opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, because the word "agent" has meant very different things depending on which community you ask, and I think it helps to look at it historically.

In the classical AI sense, like in Russell and Norvig's textbook, an agent is anything that perceives its environment and acts on it. That definition is extremely broad: a thermostat is an agent, a chess program is an agent. It's useful philosophically but doesn't tell you much about what's interesting.

Then in reinforcement learning, an agent became something more specific: a system that interacts with an environment, takes actions, gets rewards, and learns a policy to maximize return. AlphaGo and Atari agents are the canonical examples. The key point there is that the environment is usually narrow and well defined, and the agent is trained from scratch for that one environment. So you get superhuman performance on Go, but it doesn't transfer to anything else.

What I think is new in the language model era, and what I spent a lot of my PhD on with things like ReAct and the tree-of-thoughts line of work, is that the agent can now reason. Language gives you a kind of action that doesn't directly change the external world but changes the agent's own internal state. Thinking is an action. Once you have that, you can generalize across very different environments, whether it's a web page, a codebase, or a conversation, because reasoning is the common interface. That's why I'd describe a modern language agent as a system that uses language both to reason and to act in an open-ended environment.

So if I had to give one working definition, it's this: an agent is something that can make decisions over multiple steps in an environment that pushes back, where the outcome depends on what it does. The degree of "agentness" depends on how open-ended the environment is and how much autonomy the system has over a long horizon.

And honestly, I think the definition matters less than the question of what environments and tasks we evaluate on. The interesting shift right now is from asking "how smart is the model" to asking "what real-world value can it create when it's actually put to work." That's where the definition of agent becomes practical rather than academic.

r001.rationale: The response describes modern agents as reasoning and acting in open-ended environments, but it does not identify external-world interaction as the feature that distinguishes agents from text-generation-only systems in NLP research.

r002.rationale: It contrasts classical AI and reinforcement-learning meanings with language-model agents, but does not state that contemporary use commonly means systems built on large models or that this narrows the term’s broader historical meaning.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think "agent" is one of those words that means different things depending on who you ask, so let me try to pull the threads together.

If you go back to the textbook definition, from Russell and Norvig, an agent is just something that perceives its environment and takes actions in it. That's a very broad definition. A thermostat qualifies. In reinforcement learning, that framing got formalized: you have states, actions, rewards, and the agent is the policy that maps observations to actions to maximize reward. For a long time that was the dominant picture in AI research, and most of the famous agents, AlphaGo, Atari players, robotics controllers, came out of that tradition.

Then language models arrived, and the word shifted. When people in the LLM world say "agent" today, they usually mean a language model that doesn't just produce text for a human to read, but produces text that does something: calls a tool, runs code, browses the web, writes to a file, and then observes the result and keeps going. The key difference from a chatbot is that the output feeds back into an environment and the loop continues. That's essentially what we were trying to show with ReAct, that reasoning and acting can live in the same trace, and the model can interleave thinking about what to do with actually doing it.

So in my mind the cleanest unifying definition is: an agent is a system that interacts with an environment through a loop of observation and action, over multiple steps, toward some goal. The environment can be a game, a simulated world, a web browser, a terminal, a codebase, or even a conversation with a person. What changed with LLMs is not the definition, but the fact that the action space became language itself, which is extraordinarily general. The same model can act in a hundred different environments because all of them can be described in text.

I'd also add one distinction I find useful: there's agent as a research object and agent as a product. As a research object, you care about generalization, learning from feedback, how the model handles long horizons and partial information. As a product, you care about reliability, cost, and whether it actually completes a task a user cares about. A lot of confusion in current discussions comes from mixing those two. Somebody says "agents don't work" and they mean products, while somebody else says "agents are the future" and they mean the research direction. Both can be true at the same time.

And honestly, I've come to think the interesting question is less about defining the agent and more about defining the environment and the task. If you look at the history of the field, progress happened when someone built the right environment: Atari, Go, and now things like software engineering benchmarks or web tasks. The agent is a function of what you ask it to do and where it has to do it. So when someone asks me "what is an agent," I often turn it around and ask, "what's the environment, and what does success look like there?" Once you answer that, the agent part usually becomes clearer.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes an agent from a chatbot by saying its output acts on an environment and the results feed back into a continuing interaction loop.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the broad historical definition of an agent with contemporary LLM usage, which usually means a language model that acts through tools and continues based on results.

astra-6.text:
I think “agent” means slightly different things in different research communities. In reinforcement learning, an agent is something that observes an environment, takes actions, and receives rewards. The emphasis is on learning a policy through interaction. In other contexts, people might use “agent” to mean a system that can act autonomously toward a goal.

In the language model setting, I find it useful to focus on the interaction loop. A model doesn’t just receive a question and generate an answer. It can take an action—call a tool, run some code, or search for information—observe the result, and decide what to do next. The language model becomes part of a system that makes decisions over multiple steps.

So I wouldn’t draw the boundary simply at whether a system uses tools. A fixed workflow can use tools, too. The more interesting question is: which decisions does the model control? Does it choose the next action, adapt when something fails, and determine when the task is finished? That gives us a more useful way to discuss agents than treating the term as a single, universally agreed category.

r001.rationale: It contrasts answer-only generation with a model that acts through tools, code, or search, observes results, and decides what to do next.

r002.rationale: It discusses different meanings of “agent” and the language-model setting, but does not say contemporary usage commonly narrows the term to systems built on large models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “agent” means slightly different things in different research communities. In reinforcement learning, an agent is something that interacts with an environment: it takes an action, receives an observation or reward, and decides what to do next. That definition is quite broad. Even a system playing a very simple game is an agent.

In the context of language models, people often use the word to emphasize that the model can do more than produce a response. It can use tools, observe the results, and take further actions toward a goal. Instead of generating an answer in one shot, it operates in a loop.

So I tend to think of agency as a spectrum rather than a binary property. How much does the system decide for itself? How long can it act without human intervention? Can it adapt when something unexpected happens? Different research contexts emphasize different parts of that spectrum. The useful thing is to specify the environment, the actions available, and the objective, rather than assume that everyone means the same thing by “agent.”

r001.rationale: It distinguishes language-model agents from one-shot response generation by describing tool use, observing results, and taking further actions toward a goal in a loop.

r002.rationale: It discusses how “agent” is used in language-model research, but does not say contemporary usage centers on systems built on large models or narrows the term’s broader historical meaning in AI.
